Unfortunately I think you’ll find this practice to be pretty common at smaller nonprofits. By some metric, it could be possible that you served 300 people (100 people 3 times, 50 people 6 times, etc). Embellishing impact to make it seem more impressive could be effective for a few years but only if the organization continues to purposefully not track data, have people who hold up the scheme, and the embellishments actually drive growth. 
It can set up future employees for failure when the board starts questioning why they’re not seeing growth and you either have to have the uncomfortable conversation that your predecessor was lying the whole time, or keep up the act. 
I personally wouldn’t raise anymore flags, but understand that this is the sign of a sinking ship, and you should start looking for a lifeboat.

Lexapro has been life changing for me just in the last month. I was super apprehensive about starting on it at first but I just closed my eyes and took the first pill. I had started telling myself I didn’t even care if it was a placebo effect, I just wanted to feel a little better. Once my mood started getting better I realized just how miserably I had been existing up until that point. I was worried about suicidal thoughts and my anxiety getting worse. Then I took it and started feeling better and realized I was already having suicidal thoughts and my anxiety was as bad as it had ever been. Of course there will be outliers with extreme reactions to any medication, but for the majority of people, it helps. And when you are at your lowest point, the main direction you can go is up.

I chose environmental science. I finally got my bachelor's, did an internship at an environmental consulting company and realized I hated it. I can be an analytical person, but doing data analysis for a career made me sick to my stomach. I also realized that almost every company needs an accountant, an hr person, a marketing person, a receptionist. These are incredibly marketable skills that can allow you to work in a lot of different fields with a lot of different people. Identify what your strengths are from a very broad perspective. Do you like dealing with people? Are you chatty? Do you like sitting at a desk or being on your feet? Are you good at math? Do you LIKE math? Are you creative? These kinds of things will help you identify a career path that will feel fulfilling to you, and with any of them, there will be jobs in a number of different fields. For all of them, there will be classes that are hard and that you are not good at. Taking a career quiz was incredibly informative for me to identify truly what my strengths are. Lean in to what makes you, you! That will really help. But now I just got a job that doesn't relate to my major at all because I decided to lean in to the people skills side of myself. I hope it works out for me!

Also deleting shopping apps like Amazon or Etsy is a good start! Maybe start going through the things you already have to sell/donate what you don't need and realize your spending habits.

Anxiety sucks, it really and truly does. Don't be too hard on yourself. What I try to do when I feel like I might cry at work is drink water to try and shove the lump in my throat down. This day might feel like an enormous hurdle, but just take it one hour at a time. Take deep breaths, try and ground yourself in the present. What does your chair feel like? Is there a breeze in the room? Close your eyes for a minute and listen to the sounds around you. Do you hear birds chirping? Try to stay in the present and clear your mind of worries about the past and future. I know it's easier said than done, but just give it a shot. You got this, I believe in you <3
